sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid pages mega1243 (Bangladesh Lyngam) and lyng1241 (India Lyngam) and reference records 468438, 309253, 28264, 549941.
sources.note: mega1243 lists no descriptive references (only Burling 2004 overview and the SIL 2012 wordlist survey); lyng1241 lists Nagaraja 1996, Nagaraja/Sidwell/Greenhill 2013, Sidwell 2018 for classification. The Glottolog bib held by the project (_glottolog_bib/hh.bib) adds Baker 2013 (phonology, MA ANU), Khyriem 2012 (NEHU PhD), Daladier 2011, Nagaraja 2004, van Breugel 2015.
Phonology section (inventory drawn from Nagaraja 1996) has no mention of stress, accent or tone.

sources.citation: Marthong, Venial In Goodhope. 2024. Nominal constructions in Mawiang and Lyngngam varieties of Khasi: A comparative study. PhD thesis, North-Eastern Hill University. 202 pp.
sources.note: Most recent NEHU work on Lyngngam; chapter 1/2 probably includes a phonological overview that could state stress placement.

sources.citation: Nagaraja, K. S., Paul Sidwell & Simon Greenhill. 2013. A lexicostatistical study of the Khasian languages: Khasi, Pnar, Lyngngam, and War. Mon-Khmer Studies 42: 1-11.
sources.note: Lexicostatistics/phylogeny with 200-item Lyngngam list (from Nagaraja's 1988 data); nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Khyriem, Barika. 2012. A comparative study of some regional dialects of Khasi language: a lexical and phonological study. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong. 244 pp.
sources.note: Comparative phonology of eight Khasi varieties including Lyngngam; Likely has a suprasegmental/stress comparison.

sources.citation: Kim, Amy, Seung Kim, Sayed Ahmad & Mridul Sangma. 2012. The Garos of Bangladesh: A sociolinguistic survey. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2012-007. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Only Megam-specific source found: 307-item wordlists from two Megam villages (Panchgaon, Sonyasipara) and a Bangladesh Lyngngam list; p. 43 says the transcriptions 'have not undergone thorough phonological and grammatical analysis'; no stress marks in the lists and no statement on stress. Reports only 60-61% lexical similarity between Megam and Lyngngam.

sources.citation: Nagaraja, K. S. 1996. The status of Lyngngam. Mon-Khmer Studies 26: 37-50.
sources.note: Sec. 1 'Phonology' (p. 38) gives only a tentative vowel and consonant inventory with five notes on vowel length, barred i, palatal series, aspirates and fricatives; no mention of stress, accent or tone anywhere in the 14 pages (scanned of scan, no text).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.) 1904. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. II: Mon-Khmer and Siamese-Chinese families (including Khassi and Tai). Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. Section 'Lyng-ngam' in the Khassi part.
sources.note: Lyng-ngam sketch (archive.org scanned text) covers vocabulary, 'minor differences of pronunciation', articles, case prefixes, pronouns and verb morphology; nothing on stress. The general Khassi introduction has a paragraph 'Tones' about Standard Khassi only.

sources.venue: Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society

tone.quote: There are no major differences in the phonotactics of Pnar, War, Lyngngam and S. Khasi but there are major differences in their intonation systems, Khasi being the most innovative with no or little word accentuation and final accentuation of utterances.
tone.locator: p. 176, sec. 3 'Overview of some phonological features of S.Khasi and conservative Pnar, Lyngngam and War varieties', opening sentence
tone.summary: Only remark on prosody: Lyngngam, Pnar and War differ from Khasi in intonation, Khasi having little or no word accentuation; nothing is said about tone.
tone.says: Only remark on prosody: Lyngngam, Pnar and War differ from Khasi in intonation, Khasi having little or no word accentuation; nothing is said about tone.
